title: High-power nuclear propulsion for routine deep-space missions

concept.text: The innovation would be an integrated nuclear-powered spacecraft propulsion system that can deliver useful payloads through deep space over sustained missions, followed by enough successful operation to make the capability dependable and repeatable. Its defining achievement would be a working spacecraft and mission capability: a reactor, propulsion hardware and supporting systems that meet their performance and lifetime requirements together.

Two architectures fall within this concept. In nuclear thermal propulsion, reactor heat heats propellant that is expelled for thrust. In nuclear electric propulsion, reactor heat is converted into electricity that powers an electric thruster. The supplied technical evidence primarily concerns the electric route, including lithium-fed magnetoplasmadynamic plasma thrusters. These produce comparatively low, continuous thrust and can build up speed over time while using propellant efficiently; high electrical power does not by itself establish high thrust or a short journey.

For the electric route, the spacecraft must combine a sufficiently light and reliable reactor with power conversion, heat rejection, propulsion and their interfaces. Protection, shielding and controls must also fit the mission's mass and operating constraints. The central advance is making these systems work together for the required duration; separate reactor and thruster demonstrations establish only parts of that capability.

significance.text: A successful system could combine sustained propulsion, high propellant efficiency and an energy source that does not depend on strong sunlight. If the reactor, conversion equipment and thermal hardware are light and durable enough, this could reduce propellant and launch-mass burdens, support substantial payloads and make additional deep-space trajectories practical. These would be mission-level benefits: the mass saved in propellant must be assessed alongside the mass and operating demands of the nuclear propulsion system.

The revolutionary possibility is an expansion in practical mission scale and destinations. That possibility is conditional on the complete vehicle's mass, lifetime, power and thrust, and on the chosen trajectory. The reviewed conference paper explicitly treats propulsion selection as dependent on mission duration, habitat choices and operations. Neither electric propulsion's propellant efficiency nor a high-power ground test establishes that nuclear propulsion will outperform chemical propulsion on every mission, shorten every transit or lower total cost.

Downstream synthesis: dependable nuclear propulsion could support more ambitious robotic exploration and, with other advances, larger human expeditions. Routine human travel would additionally require adequate life support, crew protection, mission operations and affordable launch. Propulsion alone would therefore establish an enabling transportation capability, not routine human settlement or travel throughout the Solar System.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a flightworthy, integrated system that meets a useful deep-space mission's power, propulsion, mass and lifetime requirements simultaneously. Scaling a thruster or reactor separately does not resolve the spacecraft problem. For nuclear electric propulsion, reactor output must be converted into usable electricity, delivered to the thruster and accompanied by adequate heat rejection, with the combined equipment remaining within the vehicle's mass budget. The reviewed technical paper identifies subsystem power scaling and integrated system development as central challenges.

Endurance is a distinct barrier. A brief high-power test does not show that propulsion hardware can operate for the cumulative duration required by a mission. The reviewed conference paper identifies thruster lifetime as the largest gap between demonstrated performance and the requirement in its development context. A convincing system must sustain useful propulsion over the intended operating period while preserving the performance of its reactor, conversion equipment and thermal systems.

Engineering synthesis: shielding, protection and control requirements must be translated into a concrete spacecraft design, including their mass and effects on system operation. The supplied evidence does not provide a complete shielding or control specification, a universal acceptable system mass, or a numerical reliability threshold. Those requirements must be set for the selected payload, trajectory, operating duration and mission consequences.

The propulsion tradeoff also remains at mission scale. Electric thrusters conserve propellant by accelerating it efficiently, but their comparatively low thrust means that acceleration accumulates over time. Useful payload delivery therefore depends on the interaction of power, spacecraft mass, operating duration and trajectory. Demonstrating a power level alone leaves this mission-performance question open.

current_state.text: NASA's May 2, 2018 report describes the KRUSTY fission power experiment culminating in a 28-hour full-power ground test that simulated mission conditions. The prototype transferred reactor heat through passive sodium heat pipes to Stirling engines that generated electricity. This establishes a reported reactor-and-conversion ground demonstration. It does not establish an integrated propulsion flight, and a stated long-term design capability must not be read as evidence of a ten-year endurance test.

NASA's April 28, 2026 article reports that a lithium-fed magnetoplasmadynamic thruster reached input-power levels of up to 120 kilowatts during February 2026 testing in JPL's vacuum facility. This was a ground test of a propulsion component. The reported power level does not establish spacecraft performance, mission-duration endurance or operation with a reactor supplying the power. The article presents payload and launch-mass benefits as conditional on further development and nuclear integration.

The reviewed 19-page conference paper, IEPC-2024-841, supplies technical context on propulsion architecture, subsystem scaling and lifetime gaps. It is a development paper rather than evidence of a completed nuclear propulsion mission. Its discussion includes a statement attributed to a NASEM report; that report was encountered through the paper's quotation in the supplied review, rather than independently examined.

The retained NASA article dated October 20, 2026 describes SR-1 Freedom as a planned nuclear electric propulsion demonstration in deep space, with a planned 2028 launch. It describes integration of a fission reactor with a Brayton power conversion system. These are development plans, not a completed flight. October 20 is the article's date; the supplied review does not establish that the announcement event mentioned in the article occurred on that date.

The SR-1 article's retained version was updated November 6, 2026, after the November 1 assessment cutoff. The supplied record contains no independently recovered pre-cutoff version, so its exact wording and the availability of particular details by November 1 remain uncertain. The supplied review also contains no bounded freshness-search results establishing a comprehensive survey at that cutoff. These limits constrain conclusions about overall status; they do not negate the separately dated component reports.

Evidence boundary: the earlier research also mentioned historical nuclear thermal engine ground tests, but the supplied reviewed texts do not substantiate that historical assertion. It remains unverified within this record and cannot serve here as a documented milestone. This limitation does not establish that such tests did not occur, and it does not remove nuclear thermal propulsion from the concept's scope.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independently measure a mission-duration deep-space flight of an integrated nuclear propulsion system delivering a useful payload on a trajectory that is impractical or substantially more burdensome using an available chemical alternative. Define the payload, destination or trajectory, operating duration and success conditions before evaluation. This is a proposed completion test, not an established standard.
completion_criteria.label: Nuclear flight delivers payload on chemically impractical or burdensome trajectories

completion_criteria.text: Proposed comparison: specify the chemical alternative and the relevant measures of burden in advance, including launch mass, transit time and total mission cost where appropriate. Report the actual tradeoffs rather than requiring the nuclear system to win on every measure. The comparison should identify the conditions under which its advantage holds, including vehicle mass, power, propulsion duration and operational assumptions.
completion_criteria.label: Report chemical-alternative tradeoffs and conditions supporting the nuclear system’s advantage

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evidence package: provide independently assessable measurements of power delivered to propulsion, thrust and propellant consumption, achieved trajectory, delivered payload, cumulative operating time and degradation. Demonstrate reactor, conversion, thermal-management and propulsion operation together over the required mission duration. Report interruptions, failures and operating limits so that useful endurance can be distinguished from a short peak-power result.
completion_criteria.label: Measurements verify integrated propulsion operation over the required mission duration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed route to routine use: subsequent flights should establish repeatable payload delivery, reliability and actual operating costs under declared mission conditions. Independent reproduction or verification should be sufficient to test the principal performance claims. No particular repeat-flight count is established by the supplied evidence. A successful mission or finite series would demonstrate a bounded operating envelope; broader reliability and economic claims would require corresponding operational experience.
completion_criteria.label: Subsequent flights verify repeatable payload delivery, reliability and operating costs

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: NUC-10, Long-lived, low-intervention nuclear power for remote sites, has the closest overlap in dependable autonomous power and long operating life. NUC-04 adds spacecraft mass constraints, propulsion integration and trajectory performance. NUC-02, Mass-produced fission plants with radically lower delivered cost, shares questions of manufacturability and cost, but inexpensive terrestrial electricity does not establish a sufficiently light space propulsion system. Each remains a distinct innovation.

Roster-based synthesis: NUC-06, Reactor structural materials that remain reliable under extreme neutron exposure, and NUC-11, Durable materials and chemistry control for aggressive reactor coolants, could contribute to reactor lifetime and thermal-system durability. NUC-09, Very-high-burnup fuel with robust fission-product retention, overlaps with fuel endurance and containment. These are potential enabling advances; the supplied evidence does not establish that NUC-04 requires completion of any particular one of them.

Roster-based synthesis: NUC-08, Broadly applicable passive shutdown and long-term reactor cooling, overlaps with dependable reactor protection and heat management. NUC-12, Reliable, non-invasive, real-time three-dimensional reactor-core diagnosis, could support monitoring and control, but full three-dimensional diagnosis is not established here as a prerequisite for nuclear propulsion. NUC-05, Practical remote verification of otherwise inaccessible operating reactors, concerns obtaining credible information about reactor operation; it is distinct from a spacecraft's own controls and from demonstrating successful payload delivery.

Roster-based synthesis: NUC-01, A self-sustaining, net-electric fusion power plant, and NUC-07, Net-electric fusion using a low-neutron fuel cycle, concern different energy-generation breakthroughs. A future fusion system might be considered for propulsion, but net electricity generation alone would not establish flightworthy mass, integrated propulsion or mission endurance. The concrete reactor and propulsion developments documented in this record concern the fission-based electric route.

Roster-based synthesis: NUC-03, A scalable closed fuel cycle that consumes most long-lived actinides, and NUC-13, A fuel cycle with substantially stronger built-in proliferation resistance, address fuel-cycle outcomes rather than propulsion performance. Fuel selection and handling can intersect with spacecraft reactor design, but successful deep-space propulsion would not by itself demonstrate either actinide consumption at scale or stronger intrinsic proliferation resistance.

brief.title: Dependable nuclear-powered travel through deep space
possible: Explorers could send substantial cargo and scientific instruments on deep-space journeys that ordinary chemical rockets make impractical or burdensome. Dependable nuclear propulsion could support more ambitious robotic exploration and, alongside other advances, larger human expeditions.

Nuclear heat could directly heat propellant, the material expelled to push a spacecraft, or generate electricity for an electric engine. The breakthrough would be a complete spacecraft that delivers useful cargo and keeps doing so reliably.
why: Power that does not depend on strong sunlight could expand the destinations and routes available to spacecraft. Efficient use of propellant could leave more room for useful cargo and reduce the mass that exploration missions must launch.

sources.who: NASA and the Department of Energy’s National Nuclear Security Administration
sources.showed: A prototype reactor generated electricity during a ground experiment that ended with a 28-hour test at full power. It also handled simulated equipment failures.
sources.quote: Throughout the experiment, the team simulated power reduction, failed engines and failed heat pipes, showing that the system could continue to operate and successfully handle multiple failures.
sources.cited_for: The experiment demonstrates a reactor working with equipment that converts its heat into electricity.
sources.not_established: It did not demonstrate propulsion in flight or endurance over a deep-space mission.

sources.who: NASA JPL, Princeton University and NASA’s Glenn Research Center
sources.showed: A lithium-fed electric engine reached an input power of 120 kilowatts in a ground test.
sources.quote: During the test, the team achieved power levels of up to 120 kilowatts.
sources.cited_for: The test demonstrates a propulsion component intended for a future nuclear electric spacecraft.
sources.not_established: It did not demonstrate reactor-powered operation, mission-length endurance or useful cargo delivery.

sources.who: NASA, the Department of Energy’s Idaho National Laboratory and Sierra Lobo
sources.showed: NASA describes plans for SR-1 Freedom to demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion in deep space. Its power module would combine a reactor with equipment that converts heat into electricity.
sources.cited_for: The mission plans describe how nuclear power and electric propulsion would come together on a spacecraft.
sources.not_established: A planned mission does not establish successful operation in flight.

shown: NASA teams have demonstrated reactor electricity generation and a powerful electric engine separately on the ground. The remaining step is a complete spacecraft that sustains useful propulsion throughout a deep-space mission.
missing: A complete flight system must deliver enough power and propulsion while keeping its reactor, cooling equipment and radiation shielding light enough.
The engine and supporting systems must last through the required operating period without losing too much performance.
Repeated flights must establish dependable cargo delivery and actual operating costs.

milestones.label: A nuclear-powered flight delivers cargo on a demanding route
milestones.explanation: A complete nuclear-powered spacecraft would have to deliver useful cargo on a predefined route that chemical rockets make impractical or substantially more burdensome. This would establish a useful mission capability.

milestones.label: A comparison establishes where nuclear propulsion has an advantage
milestones.explanation: A comparison would have to report tradeoffs against a chemical alternative chosen in advance, including relevant mass, time and cost measures. This would establish the conditions under which nuclear propulsion helps.

milestones.label: Measurements confirm sustained operation of the complete system
milestones.explanation: Independent assessment would have to confirm power, push, propellant use, route, cargo delivery, operating time, wear and failures across the required mission duration. This would establish endurance of all systems working together.

milestones.label: Further flights establish repeatable delivery and operating costs
milestones.explanation: Subsequent flights would have to establish repeatable cargo delivery, reliability and actual operating costs under stated conditions, with independent verification. This would define the missions the system can serve dependably.

uncertain: Acceptable spacecraft mass, radiation shielding, controls, lifetime and reliability depend on the chosen mission and remain undefined.
The demonstration’s cargo, route, chemical alternative, cost boundaries and required number of repeat flights remain undecided.
High electrical power alone does not establish strong push or a shorter journey; electric engines build speed gradually.

page.title: Nuclear propulsion for deep-space missions
page.definition: A spacecraft successfully uses a fission reactor for propulsion during a mission beyond Earth orbit. Nuclear thermal propulsion heats propellant directly; nuclear electric propulsion converts reactor heat into electricity for thrusters that accelerate propellant, the material expelled to produce thrust.

goal.need: NASEM describes long-stay crewed Mars missions lasting about 900 days, with travel legs of 180–210 days each. Short-stay missions last 400–750 days but require greater velocity changes and more propellant. NASA commissioned nuclear-propulsion assessments against a total crew mission duration of no more than 750 days.

figures.caption: Crewed Mars mission durations described by NASEM.
figures.note: Durations include travel and time at Mars.

statements.body: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, Space Nuclear Propulsion Technologies Committee
statements.quote: the committee also recommends that NASA use these cargo missions as a means of flight qualification of the space nuclear propulsion system
statements.context: The recommendation concerns cargo missions preceding the report’s baseline crewed Mars mission and covers thermal and electric propulsion.

statements.quote: this mission will demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion in deep space

completion.title: A complete nuclear propulsion system operates successfully during an actual deep-space mission.
completion.criterion: The final nuclear propulsion system satisfies NASA technology readiness level 9: successful operation during an actual mission beyond Earth orbit. Reactor heat must produce propulsion directly, or reactor-generated electricity must power the electric thrusters. Performance and operating duration are assessed against that mission’s requirements; the readiness criterion specifies no universal power, thrust, payload or lifetime.
completion.set_by: NASA, NPR 7123.1D, Appendix E, TRL 9; NASA’s SR-1 programme supplies the beyond-Earth-orbit mission setting.
completion.threshold_quote: The final product is successfully operated in an actual mission.
completion.basis: NASA’s endpoint is successful operation of the final system. Polzin and colleagues explicitly apply TRL 9 to space nuclear systems after at least one successful operational mission. This supports a mission-proven capability. Neither source defines how many flights establish routine service.

milestones.title: A nuclear propulsion component demonstrates its basic function in a laboratory.
milestones.criterion: NASA TRL 4 requires laboratory hardware to demonstrate basic functionality with performance agreeing with predictions. Electric-route evidence: one lithium-fed magnetoplasmadynamic thruster underwent five ignitions on 24 February 2026 and reached 120 kW input power. NASA’s 28 April 2026 report is not peer reviewed; it does not establish mission endurance or a complete nuclear propulsion system’s readiness.
milestones.set_by: NASA, NPR 7123.1D, Appendix E, tabulated TRL 4 criterion.

milestones.title: A nuclear propulsion prototype demonstrates performance under critical environmental conditions.
milestones.criterion: NASA TRL 6 requires high-fidelity system/subsystem prototypes that address critical scaling issues and demonstrate performance in a relevant environment. Thermal heritage: one NERVA XE engine completed 28 startup/shutdown cycles in 1969. Electric-power heritage: one KRUSTY reactor/converter prototype underwent a 28-hour ground test beginning on 20 March 2018, at varying temperatures and power levels. KRUSTY did not include propulsion. Neither result certifies a present deep-space vehicle at TRL 6.
milestones.set_by: NASA, NPR 7123.1D, Appendix E, tabulated TRL 6 criterion.

milestones.title: A nuclear propulsion prototype functions on its spacecraft in the actual operating environment.
milestones.criterion: NASA TRL 7 requires a high-fidelity prototype to function on its intended platform in the actual operational environment. For this capability, that means propulsion operation in space. This demonstration step is conditional: NASA permits progression from TRL 6 to TRL 8 when a separate demonstration is unnecessary for risk reduction. NASA’s article of 20 October 2026 describes SR-1 as a planned electric-propulsion demonstration.
milestones.set_by: NASA, NPR 7123.1D, Appendix E, tabulated TRL 7 criterion.

milestones.title: The final nuclear propulsion system passes flight qualification for its intended mission.
milestones.criterion: NASA TRL 8 requires final-configuration hardware to pass qualification through test and analysis for its intended environment and platform, with necessary life testing complete. For a nuclear propulsion system, qualification concerns the complete operational configuration, including its reactor and propulsion interfaces. Qualification of an individual reactor, converter or thruster does not establish qualification of the complete system.
milestones.set_by: NASA, NPR 7123.1D, Appendix E, TRL 8, hardware description and example 1.
milestones.threshold_quote: the final product is qualified for the operational environment through test and analysis.

not_found: No universal power, thrust, lifetime, payload or repeat-flight threshold for routine deep-space nuclear propulsion was found in NASA programme pages, NASA readiness criteria or the NASEM Mars-propulsion report.
No flight-qualification result for a complete deep-space nuclear propulsion system was found in the programme and technical sources searched.
No peer-reviewed paper reporting the 24 February 2026 JPL lithium-thruster result was located.

results.finding: One KRUSTY reactor-converter prototype completed a 28-hour full-power laboratory test.
results.detail: The reactor converted fission heat to electricity, and the team reported that the system worked as designed. It did not include a thruster.
results.quote: The experiment culminated with a 28-hour, full-power test that simulated a mission, including reactor startup, ramp to full power, steady operation and shutdown.

results.finding: One KRUSTY reactor-converter prototype completed a 28-hour full-power test simulating a mission.
results.detail: The test exercised a reactor and power converter, including simulated failures, but did not demonstrate an integrated propulsion system.
results.quote: The experiment culminated with a 28-hour, full-power test that simulated a mission, including reactor startup, ramp to full power, steady operation and shutdown.

results.finding: One lithium-fed MPD thruster prototype reached 120 kW in a laboratory test.
results.detail: The thruster operated through five ignitions and reached its target power. The test did not demonstrate mission endurance or a complete nuclear propulsion system.
results.quote: During the test, the team achieved power levels of up to 120 kilowatts.

results.finding: A lithium MPD thruster (one described) operated for approximately 500 hours in a bench test.
results.detail: Bench tests also found thrust varied quadratically with discharge current, as predicted by the engineering model. The text identifies a journal article but does not state whether it was peer reviewed.
results.quote: При потребляемой мощности 450–500 кВт двигатель в стационарном режиме работал ~500 ч, при этом он сохранял работоспособность и рабочие параметры.

results.finding: One NERVA XE-Prime flight-geometry nuclear thermal engine achieved 244750 N thrust in a ground test.
results.detail: The report describes a successful firing at the Nevada test station, but the excerpt does not establish that the prototype addressed critical scaling issues or met all TRL 6 requirements.
results.quote:
culminating with the successful firing of a flight geometry
engine labeled XE-Prime which achieved 244750 N (55000 lb)
thrust.

results.finding: One nuclear thermal propulsion reactor prototype recorded a maximum pressure vibration of 1.9 psirms during cold-flow testing.
results.detail: The non-nuclear test approximated predicted operating flow conditions except at the fuel outlet. It did not control temperature or demonstrate a complete propulsion system in a relevant thermal environment.
results.quote:
Maximum values encountered 
were 1.9 psirms and 4.2 grms in the 
inlet plenum and on the exterior 
head of the EDU, respectively

results.finding: One KRUSTY reactor and converter prototype operated for 28 consecutive hours.
results.detail: The ground test varied temperature and power and examined transients. It demonstrated a power subsystem but did not include propulsion or establish TRL 6 for a deep-space vehicle.
results.quote:
This paper presents results from the KRUSTY nuclear
system test, which operated the power system at various temperatures and power levels for 28 consecutive
hours.

results.finding: One Plazma-A spacecraft carried an SPT-70 electric propulsion system during space tests in 1986.
results.detail: The spacecraft had a thermionic nuclear power unit, and the thruster cathode operated in a state of readiness for firing. The passage does not explicitly report that the thruster fired in space or that the nuclear unit powered it.
results.quote:
В 1986 году  проведены космические испытания  ЭРДУ с СПД- 70 в составе КА 
«Плазма-А» с термоэмиссионной ядерной энергоустановкой ТЭУ -5.

results.finding: One MPD thruster operated for approximately 500 hours in a ground life test.
results.detail: The lithium thruster retained its operating parameters at 450–500 kW. The test ended because the test stand failed; the text does not establish a reactor-integrated propulsion prototype.
results.quote: При потребляемой мощности 450–500 кВт двигатель в стационарном режиме работал ~500 ч, при этом он сохранял работоспособность и рабочие параметры.

results.finding: One MPD thruster prototype operated in space at approximately 17 kW.
results.detail: The prototype ran for several minutes outside Kosmos-869, powered by batteries. It was not demonstrated as a reactor-powered propulsion system on its intended spacecraft.
results.quote: ГП прекрасно проработал несколько минут на номинальном режиме, на мощности ~17 кВт.

results.finding: One KIWI A3 reactor operated at an average power of 112.5 MW in a ground test.
results.detail: The measured power was 22% above the designed level, and the core sustained structural damage. The report does not establish agreement with predictions as required by the criterion.
results.quote:
It was later determined that through calibration errors in
the neutronic power measuring system, the reactor was
actually operated at an average power level of 112.5 MW for
259 seconds.

results.finding: One experimental reactor unit reached a maximum inlet-plenum pressure vibration of 1.9 psirms in cold-flow testing.
results.detail: The non-nuclear surrogate tested flow and vibration behavior, but did not demonstrate propellant heating or establish that component performance agreed with predictions. Further model correlation is planned.
results.quote:
Maximum values encountered 
were 1.9 psirms and 4.2 grms in the 
inlet plenum and on the exterior 
head of the EDU, respectively

results.finding: One KRUSTY reactor power system operated for 28 consecutive hours.
results.detail: The ground test demonstrated a reactor and power conversion system operating as expected. It did not include an electric thruster.
results.quote:
This paper presents results from the KRUSTY nuclear
system test, which operated the power system at various temperatures and power levels for 28 consecutive
hours. The testing showed that the system operated as expected and that the reactor is highly tolerant of
possible failure conditions and transients.

results.finding: Topaz was flight-tested on 2 spacecraft and supplied electricity to an electric-propulsion subsystem.
results.detail: The source does not explicitly state that the propulsion subsystem operated to produce thrust in space.
results.quote:
The world‘s first NPP ‘Topol” using thermionic energy conversion and providing 5 kWe of power, well-known as 
‘Topaz”, was tested in flight on two spacecraft in 1987-1988. Electricity from the Topaz system was used to power 
an electric propulsion (EP) subsystem.
